interactions.label: Why does N-acetylcysteine (NAC) effectively treat paracetamol overdose?

params.question: Why does N-acetylcysteine (NAC) effectively treat paracetamol overdose?

answers.text: It directly inactivates paracetamol in the gastrointestinal tract before absorption

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: NAC does not prevent absorption. It acts at the hepatic level, serving as a cysteine precursor to replenish the glutathione stores that the toxic metabolite NAPQI depletes.

answers.text: It replenishes hepatic glutathione, restoring the liver's defence against NAPQI-mediated oxidative damage

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: At toxic doses, CYP2E1 converts excess paracetamol to NAPQI, which depletes glutathione. NAC provides cysteine for glutathione resynthesis, directly countering the mechanism of hepatotoxicity.

answers.text: It inhibits CYP2E1, preventing the formation of the toxic metabolite NAPQI

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: NAC does not inhibit CYP2E1. It works downstream of NAPQI formation by replenishing the glutathione that NAPQI consumes.

answers.text: It accelerates renal excretion of paracetamol, reducing the hepatic load

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: NAC does not enhance renal clearance. It acts within hepatocytes by replenishing glutathione — the antioxidant defence that NAPQI destroys.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the pathway: CYP2E1 converts excess paracetamol to NAPQI → NAPQI depletes hepatic glutathione → oxidative hepatocellular necrosis. NAC replenishes glutathione, restoring the liver's antioxidant defence.
Well done! NAC replenishes glutathione — the direct antidote to NAPQI-mediated hepatotoxicity. This is the paradigm example of xenobiotic-induced oxidative liver injury.

params.question: Which of the following best explains why mitochondria are the primary intracellular source of reactive oxygen species?

answers.text: Mitochondria contain high concentrations of iron, which catalyses hydroxyl radical formation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While iron can catalyse free radical reactions via the Fenton reaction, the primary mechanism is electron leakage from the electron transport chain, not iron-catalysed reactions.

answers.text: About 1–2% of electrons leak from the electron transport chain and partially reduce oxygen to superoxide

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Instead of completing the four-electron reduction of O₂ to water, leaked electrons perform a one-electron reduction, generating the superoxide radical — the starting point of most reactive oxygen species.

answers.text: Mitochondria lack antioxidant enzymes, so any ROS generated accumulates unchecked

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Mitochondria do contain antioxidant enzymes such as manganese superoxide dismutase. The issue is not absent defences but the continuous generation of superoxide through ETC electron leakage.

answers.text: The low pH of the mitochondrial matrix promotes spontaneous oxidation of membrane lipids

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The mitochondrial matrix is actually alkaline (~pH 8), not acidic. ROS generation is driven by electron leakage from the respiratory chain during oxidative phosphorylation.

overallFeedback.feedback: About 1–2% of electrons leak from the electron transport chain. Instead of fully reducing O₂ to water, they generate superoxide — making mitochondria the primary intracellular ROS source.
Correct! Mitochondrial ETC electron leakage (1–2%) is the main physiological source of ROS, making mitochondria central to both normal redox signalling and oxidative stress.

interactions.label: In atherosclerosis, why do macrophages in the artery wall accumulate cholesterol

params.question: In atherosclerosis, why do macrophages in the artery wall accumulate cholesterol without limit after taking up oxidised LDL?

answers.text: Oxidised LDL contains a higher concentration of cholesterol esters than native LDL

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The cholesterol content of oxidised LDL is not the issue. The key mechanism is the unregulated uptake through scavenger receptors, which lack the feedback control present on normal LDL receptors.

answers.text: Scavenger receptors that take up oxidised LDL lack the feedback regulation that controls native LDL receptor uptake

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Unlike the native LDL receptor (which is downregulated when intracellular cholesterol rises), scavenger receptors have no such feedback. Macrophages therefore continue engulfing oxidised LDL, become engorged with cholesterol, and transform into foam cells.

answers.text: Macrophages in the artery wall lose their ability to synthesise cholesterol esterase for cholesterol breakdown

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The problem is not impaired cholesterol processing but uncontrolled uptake. Scavenger receptors lack feedback regulation, so macrophages keep internalising oxidised LDL until they become foam cells.

answers.text: Oxidised LDL inhibits macrophage apoptosis, allowing indefinite cholesterol accumulation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The narration identifies the mechanism as unregulated scavenger receptor uptake — not inhibition of apoptosis. Without feedback control, cholesterol accumulates and foam cells form, eventually building into atherosclerotic plaques.

overallFeedback.feedback: When LDL enters the artery wall and becomes oxidised, macrophages take it up via scavenger receptors that have no feedback regulation. This uncontrolled uptake causes cholesterol to accumulate, transforming macrophages into foam cells — the hallmark of early atherosclerosis.

Excellent! The absence of feedback control on scavenger receptors is the critical difference from normal LDL uptake, and it explains why oxidised LDL — not native LDL — drives foam cell formation and plaque progression.
